name: Sam Altman

education.notes: Dropped out after ~2 years to focus on Loopt — the classic 'Stanford dropout founder' narrative.

keyDecisions: Got into Stanford CS — credentialing event for what came next.
lessons: The Stanford CS network was an asset he leveraged across all subsequent chapters.

keyDecisions: Founded location-sharing app at 19, in Y Combinator's first (Summer 2005) cohort.
Raised ~$40M+ from Sequoia, NEA, and others over the company's life.
Persisted for 7 years through changing platforms (BREW → smartphone era) without finding clear PMF.
lessons: High-profile funding does not equal product-market fit. Loopt looked successful for years while burning cash on a product nobody really needed.
Network access (YC cohort 1, top-tier VCs) bought a long runway despite a weak idea.
The exit looked like 'success' externally but was effectively flat vs total capital raised.
careerSteps.notes: Acquired by Green Dot Corporation for ~$43M in March 2012 — roughly equal to total raised. Not a real financial win for investors or for Altman as founder (vs his subsequent chapters).

keyDecisions: Took over YC presidency from Paul Graham — based on PG's personal trust, not Loopt's commercial success.
Pushed YC into harder-tech areas (YC Research, which spun out OpenAI in 2015).
Made angel investments that compounded significantly (Reddit, Stripe, Airbnb era).
lessons: The YC presidency was the highest-leverage seat in startups for a decade — and his access to it came VIA PG's trust (a Loopt-era YC relationship), NOT via Loopt's results.
This is the chapter where Altman's wealth + influence actually began compounding — not the founding chapter.
careerSteps.notes: Read this carefully: if you strip out the YC presidency from Altman's career, his Loopt outcome alone would not have produced the wealth or platform he has today.

keyDecisions: Took OpenAI from research lab to commercial powerhouse.
Engineered the Microsoft partnership (2019 → $1B initial, then $10B+).
Survived November 2023 board firing and was reinstated within a week — coalitional power play.
lessons: Coalitional power (Microsoft, employees, media) was the actual moat in the 2023 board crisis.
Operating a frontier AI lab in the AI-revolution era is the single highest-leverage CEO seat in tech right now.
careerSteps.notes: Pivotal figure in the AI revolution. Net worth has surged through OpenAI's various structures (though direct equity is famously complex — he has publicly stated he didn't take OpenAI equity for years).

exitEvents.notes: Loopt → Green Dot. Roughly flat vs ~$40M+ capital raised — not a real founder win.

outcomes.currentStatus: CEO of OpenAI. One of the most powerful people in tech globally. Wealth + influence largely derive from his time at YC (the network) and OpenAI (the AI-revolution seat), NOT from his founding career at Loopt.

lessons.lesson: Headline founder success can disguise where wealth actually came from. Altman's wealth comes from network access (YC → OpenAI), not from being a great founder of Loopt.
Funding raised is a vanity metric. Loopt raised heavily and exited flat. Do not pattern-match 'raised a lot' as success.
Network effects compound across roles — being in the right rooms for a decade matters more than the specific job title at any one point.
Stanford CS + YC cohort 1 + PG's trust were the structural advantages. You can't replicate his path without something equivalent.

sources.title: Sam Altman — Wikipedia (entry point; verify primary sources)

notes: TIER 2 — CAUTIONARY TALE. The headline 'Altman is a successful young founder' obscures the actual mechanism (YC presidency → OpenAI CEO, both granted through network access, not Loopt's product success). Pattern-matching to him is dangerous unless you also have his network access. He is in the corpus *as the canonical example* of how to read 3D-not-2D.
